result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.chromatic_number_upper_bound()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get an upper bound on the chromatic number from a coloring. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L34558-L34630){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.chromatic_number_upper_bound(coloring=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Chromatic number upper bound](/assets/graphs/chromatic-number-upper-bound.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A five-node graph colored greedily so that no edge joins two nodes of the same color: C and E get color 0 (accent), A and D color 1 (teal), B color 2 (violet). The card counts three colors used, the upper bound 3." width="100%"} The chromatic number is the minimum number of colors needed to color a graph so that no two adjacent nodes share a color. Computing it exactly is NP-hard, but any valid coloring gives an upper bound: if a coloring uses `k` colors, the chromatic number is at most `k`. This method returns the number of distinct colors in a coloring. This is useful for: - estimating how many time slots, frequencies, or resources a conflict graph needs - comparing coloring strategies (fewer colors means a tighter bound) - quickly checking whether a graph might be 2- or 3-colorable The bound is only as good as the coloring. With no argument, the method runs `greedy_color()` with its default `"largest_first"` strategy; passing a coloring from a stronger strategy such as `"dsatur"` can give a tighter bound. When a coloring is supplied, it is *not* checked for validity, so pass it through `is_valid_coloring()` first if it did not come from `greedy_color()`; an invalid coloring does not give a true upper bound. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [coloring]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [dict[int, int] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : A dictionary mapping node IDs to integer colors, typically the output of `greedy_color()`. Only the number of distinct values is used. If `None` (the default), a greedy coloring is computed first using the `"largest_first"` strategy. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The number of distinct colors used in the coloring (`0` for an empty coloring or an empty graph). ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A triangle requires 3 mutually distinct colors, so its chromatic number (and the upper bound this method returns) is exactly 3: ::: {#07e9a2cb .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) # Get upper bound using a default greedy coloring graph.chromatic_number_upper_bound() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: Supplying a coloring from a different strategy can tighten the bound. On this random graph the default coloring gives 5, while a DSATUR coloring proves that 4 colors suffice: ::: {#f3389de8 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_gnm_graph(n=30, m=80, seed=23) dsatur = graph.greedy_color(strategy="dsatur") (graph.chromatic_number_upper_bound(), graph.chromatic_number_upper_bound(dsatur)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (5, 4) ``` ::: :::
